stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A county wildlife agency wants to estimate the proportion of the county's 900 ponds that contain invasive American bullfrogs. The agency mailed a notice to the owners of all 900 ponds asking them to report whether bullfrogs were present, "especially if you have seen or heard bullfrogs this year." The owners of 60 ponds replied, and 45 of those 60 ponds, or 75%, were reported to contain bullfrogs.
choices: Since 75% is well above half, most of the county's 900 ponds very likely contain bullfrogs.
The estimate is unreliable mainly because 60 ponds is too few out of the county's 900 ponds.
Because owners chose whether to reply to a notice about bullfrogs, the 75% may not represent all 900 ponds.
A sample of ponds whose owners did not reply would give a representative estimate for all 900 ponds.
explanation: The agency wants to learn about all 900 ponds, but the ponds in the sample were the ones whose owners decided to reply. The notice specifically invited replies from owners who had seen or heard bullfrogs, so ponds with bullfrogs were probably more likely to be included. A self-selected sample like this is not random, so the 75% may not represent the county's ponds and could be biased upward.

A.why: You treated a clear majority in a biased sample as proof about the whole population. A large percentage can't make up for owners selecting themselves, especially when the notice encouraged owners with bullfrogs to reply.

B.why: You blamed the sample size instead of how the sample was chosen. A random sample of 60 ponds could give a reasonable estimate. The real problem is that these 60 owners chose to reply.

D.why: You swapped one unrepresentative group for its opposite. Ponds whose owners didn't reply are also a special subgroup, probably tilted toward ponds without bullfrogs, so they don't represent all 900 ponds either.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A city's water department wants to know what percent of the city's residents support a new monthly fee to pay for storm-drain upgrades. The department held an evening public meeting about street flooding at a community center in the Riverside neighborhood, which floods more often than any other part of the city. All 1,200 people who attended the meeting were surveyed, and 80% of them said they support the fee.
choices: With 1,200 people surveyed, the sample is large enough to show that about 80% of all city residents support the fee.
About 80% of Riverside's residents support the fee, since the survey took place inside the Riverside neighborhood.
The people surveyed chose to attend a meeting about flooding, so the results may not represent the city's residents.
Surveying an equal number of residents from neighborhoods that rarely flood would make the results represent the city.
explanation: The department wants to learn about all city residents, but the sample was everyone who chose to attend a flooding meeting in the neighborhood that floods most. These people have an obvious stake in the question, and they were not randomly selected from any population. Because the sample is self-selected and unrepresentative, the 80% may be biased and can't be generalized to the city.

A.why: You let the large sample size cover for a biased method. Surveying 1,200 self-selected attendees still gives a biased result. A bigger sample doesn't fix how the sample was chosen.

B.why: You narrowed the population to Riverside, but even that isn't justified. The attendees chose to come to a flooding meeting and may not all live in Riverside, so they are not a random sample of Riverside's residents either.

D.why: You accepted a fix that adds another non-random group. Combining attendees with residents of low-flood areas still doesn't produce a random sample, and the two groups wouldn't be weighted to match the city's population.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A folklorist wants to estimate the proportion of adults living in a mountain region who can retell, from memory, a traditional local tale about a shepherd and a talking river. The regional storytelling society has 4,000 adult members. The folklorist randomly selected 300 of these members and asked each to retell the tale. Of the 300 members, 270, or 90%, were able to do so.
choices: Since the 300 members were selected at random, about 90% of the region's adults can likely retell the tale.
Since all 300 people were storytelling society members, the sample likely does not represent the region's adults.
Since 300 people is a small number for a whole region, the sample likely does not represent the region's adults.
A random sample of adults who are not society members would likely represent all of the region's adults.
explanation: The population of interest is all adults in the region, but the sample was drawn only from storytelling society members, a group especially likely to know traditional tales. The random selection lets the folklorist generalize to society members, not to the region's adults. Because the sample comes from a special subgroup, it is unrepresentative and the 90% is likely biased upward for the region.

A.why: You saw "randomly selected" and stopped there. The members were chosen at random from the society, not from the region, so the result applies only to society members.

C.why: You blamed the sample size instead of where the sample came from. A random sample of 300 of the region's adults could support a reasonable estimate. The flaw is that only society members could be chosen.

D.why: You swapped one subgroup for its opposite. Adults outside the society leave out the members, so that sample would also be unrepresentative and would likely be biased downward.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A linguist wants to estimate the percent of the country's secondary school students who use the slang word "zonked" in everyday speech. The linguist posted a poll on a popular video channel devoted to new slang, inviting viewers who are secondary school students to answer. Of the 2,000 students who answered, 1,280, or 64%, said they use the word.
choices: Because the poll received 2,000 answers, the 64% estimate is very likely close to the true percent for the country's students.
Because the students chose to answer a poll on a slang channel, the 64% estimate may not represent the country's students.
Because most answers probably came from cities, adding more answers from rural students would make the 64% estimate representative.
Because 64% of students said they use the word, about 36% of the country's secondary school students do not use it.
explanation: The linguist wants to learn about all of the country's secondary school students, but the sample was made up of slang-channel viewers who chose to respond. Students who follow new slang and opt into a slang poll are probably more likely to use the word. This self-selected sample is not random, so the 64% may be biased and can't be generalized to all of the country's students.

A.why: You trusted the size of the sample instead of checking how it was chosen. Two thousand self-selected viewers still form a biased sample, and more answers of that kind don't reduce the bias.

C.why: You fixed one possible imbalance but left the main flaw in place. Rural or urban, every respondent is still a slang-channel viewer who chose to answer, so the sample is still self-selected.

D.why: You took the complement of a biased figure and applied it to every student in the country. If 64% doesn't represent the country's students, then 36% doesn't either.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
stimulus: A county health department wants to estimate the percent of the county's adults who have received this season's flu vaccine. During one week in October, staff members stood outside the county's pharmacies and randomly selected 500 adults from the people leaving the pharmacies. Of those 500 adults, 350, or 70%, said they had received this season's flu vaccine.
choices: Since the 500 adults were selected at random, the 70% estimate applies to all of the county's adults.
Since pharmacy visitors may be more likely to be vaccinated, the 70% estimate is likely biased.
Since 500 adults is a small sample, surveying 1,000 pharmacy visitors would remove the bias.
Since a hospital serves all kinds of adults, surveying at a hospital would remove the bias.
explanation: The department wants to learn about all of the county's adults, but the sample came only from people leaving pharmacies, where flu vaccines are often given. Selecting people at random from that location doesn't make them a random sample of the county. Pharmacy visitors are a convenience group that is probably more likely to be vaccinated, so the 70% estimate is likely biased upward.

A.why: You let the word "random" carry the result to the whole county. The adults were chosen at random only from pharmacy visitors, so the estimate can't be generalized beyond that group.

C.why: You blamed the sample size instead of how the sample was chosen. Doubling the number of pharmacy visitors gives a more precise estimate of the same biased group. It doesn't remove the bias.

D.why: You swapped one convenience location for another. Hospital visitors are also an unrepresentative subgroup, and their vaccination rate may differ from the county's in its own way.
